newsitem.title: UK: Rampant oil price sounds inflation alarm.
newsitem.headline: Rampant oil price sounds inflation alarm.

text.p: Soaring oil prices could reignite dormant inflationary pressures across the world's leading industrial nations earlier than expected as crude markets near six-year highs approaching winter, economists and analysts said.

Producer and consumer price indices in the United States and other leading economies could rise as oil's strength filters through to other energy components in inflation baskets, said investment bank Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in a report.
"This bullish oil price scenario obviously has negative implications for the future path of inflation across the major economies," the bank said.

Assuming crude stays between $22 and $24 a barrel for the next three months, "estimates...show that the biggest increase in inflation would be in France and the U.S., increasing by 0.7 and 0.6 percentage points respectively."

World oil prices on Tuesday extended the storming bull run which has pushed crude values up 40 percent in the last four months, leaving benchmark Brent crude at $25 a barrel, $9 above year-ago levels.
"Certainly this could bring an end to current falling inflation," said Stephen Schneider at investment bank Paribas in Frankfurt.

Federal Statistics Office data released Tuesday showed German September wholesale prices actually eased as sharp falls in food and nonferrous metals more than offset rising fuel prices but Schneider said the picture would change.
"Indeed, if it continues we'll have not only the first round effect on oil products directly but also on things which are produced from oil like chemicals and plastics," he said.

Germany, Europe's biggest oil importer, would not be alone in suffering the impact of the highest crude price since the 1990-1991 Gulf crisis. The previous peak was in the wake of the 1979 Iranian revolution.
"We have highlighted that this is starting to feed through. We're going to get higher airfares in the U.S. and we've already seen it in the U.K. figures," said DMG's Michael Lewis.
Britain, a net exporter of oil, is starting to feel the pinch. September saw the first rise in factory output price inflation for 14 months as a direct consequence of the oil market rally.

"The steady rise in the oil price seen through 1996 is starting to impact on the UK inflation data...with more to feed through in the coming months," said investment bank HSBC James Capel in a report published on Tuesday.
Reduced dependency on oil means the impact will be modest compared with the price shocks of the 1970s and early 1980s, but there are few signs of the pressure easing in the short-term.

"Instead of being way below expectations, which has been happening in some Scandinavia countries and Germany, we could well be in line for some slightly higher (inflation) numbers but still the outlook is quite benign," said Lewis.

Analysts said surging OECD demand for oil -- nearly 2.5 percent up on last year according to Washington-based consultants Petroleum Finance Co -- tensions in the Middle East and severely depleted heating oil stocks ahead of the northern winter add up to a bullish fundamental picture.
"The oil market looks set to remain tight through the coming winter," said Leo Drollas, chief economist at the Centre for Global Energy Studies in London.
Japanese refiners on Tuesday announced hefty increases in wholesale oil product prices for November, due to persistent crude market strength and the weakening yen against the dollar.
